summary: Describes security extensions to the Licklider Transmission Protocol, which acts as a reliable convergence layer over single-hop deep-space radio links. LTP sends data and asks for selective acknowledgments, and it is stateful with no negotiation or handshakes. The extensions add protection, and the document is experimental.

eli5.summary: Space messages can be listened to or faked. This adds seals and secret codes to those messages, so the receiver can trust where they came from and that no one changed them.

questions: how to secure deep space communication
subtitle: Authentication and integrity for Licklider Transmission Protocol used in deep-space communication.

tldr.problem: The Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP) is used for reliable communication over deep-space radio links where round-trip times are measured in minutes. LTP has no built-in authentication, making it vulnerable to eavesdropping and message forgery.
tldr.mechanism: LTP Security Extensions add two optional features: a cryptographic authentication extension that computes a MAC or digital signature over each segment (using HMAC-SHA1-80, RSA-SHA256, or a NULL checksum), and a cookie mechanism that makes denial-of-service attacks harder by requiring sessions to include a secret cookie value.
tldr.outcome: LTP can now provide origin authentication and detect tampering. However, key management in delay-tolerant networks remains an open research problem, and the extensions are experimental.

today: RFC 5327 is experimental and produced by the Delay Tolerant Networking Research Group. It provides optional security extensions for LTP but does not solve key management in DTN, which remains a research problem. Deep-space missions may use these extensions if they pre-load keys during spacecraft preparation, but widespread deployment has not occurred.

sections.title: LTP and Deep-Space Communication
sections.content:
The Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP) is designed for reliable communication over extremely long-latency, intermittently-connected links such as deep-space radio links. Round-trip times can be measured in minutes or hours, making traditional protocols like TCP impractical. LTP operates as a convergence layer, accepting data from upper layers and ensuring delivery through selective acknowledgment-based retransmission.

However, LTP as originally defined has no security features. This document adds two optional extensions: LTP Authentication, which provides cryptographic authentication of segments, and a Cookie Mechanism, which provides denial-of-service resistance. These extensions are experimental and do not address key management, which remains an open research problem in delay-tolerant networking (DTN). The extensions recognize that IPsec cannot work in these environments (IKE requires rapid key exchanges incompatible with high latencies).
sections.eli5: Space probes billions of miles away need to send data back to Earth, but the signal takes minutes to arrive. A simple protocol called LTP makes sure the data gets there. But anyone listening can read or forge messages. This adds security seals and magic cookies to prove who is sending and that messages are fresh.

sections.title: LTP Authentication Extension
sections.content:
The LTP authentication extension provides cryptographic authentication of LTP segments. It uses extension tags carried in the LTP segment header and trailer. The ciphersuite and optional key identifier are carried in the header extensions; the authentication value (MAC or signature) is carried in the trailer extensions.

The RFC defines three ciphersuites. HMAC-SHA1-80 uses HMAC with SHA-1, producing a 10-octet fixed-width authentication value. RSA-SHA256 uses RSA with SHA-256, producing a signature of variable length (e.g., 128 octets for a 1024-bit key). NULL is the same as HMAC-SHA1-80 but uses a hardcoded key, effectively providing only a checksum without authentication.

For all ciphersuites, the input to the cryptographic operation is the entire encoded LTP segment including the authentication extension tag and length, but excluding the authentication value itself. The ciphersuite number is one octet (values 0-255), with 0-127 assigned or reserved, 128-191 reserved for future use, 192-254 for private/experimental use, and 255 for the NULL ciphersuite.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a secret signature that only the sender and receiver know. The signature can be made with a shared secret (HMAC), or with a private key the receiver trusts (RSA). The receiver checks the signature to make sure the message came from the real sender and has not been changed.

sections.title: Cookie Mechanism for Denial-of-Service Resistance
sections.content:
The cookie mechanism is a well-known defense against denial-of-service attacks. A cookie is a random string of sufficient length, carried in a header extension field with tag 0x01. An LTP engine can insert a cookie into a segment at any time. After the first cookie is seen in a session, all subsequent segments in both directions MUST contain a valid cookie. A valid cookie is one that either matches the current stored cookie value or is a fresh new cookie from the peer.

The cookie value can be extended at any time by concatenating more random bits. This allows both sides to contribute to the randomness and lets either side increase the cookie length if needed. The cookie is tied to a specific LTP session and does not outlast it. If both sides emit initial cookies before seeing the peer's cookie, two cookies MUST be included in all subsequent segments (one sent, one to-be-checked). Segments with incorrect or missing cookies (after the initial grace period) MUST be silently discarded.
sections.eli5: Before talking, one side says "from now on, all messages must include this secret password." Once the other side gets it and starts including it, an attacker cannot send fake messages without knowing the password. If the password gets old, either side can pick a new one and add it to the old one, making it longer and harder to guess.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The RFC notes that for environments where the lower layers provide neither integrity nor freshness (typical of deep-space RF links), both extensions (authentication and cookie) should be used together. However, the extensions do not address key management. In delay-tolerant networks, keys must be pre-shared or established through out-of-band means, since IKE-style protocols with multiple round trips are impractical.

Regarding cryptographic algorithms: while there were concerns about SHA-1 collisions, HMAC with SHA-1 is still considered safe for authentication. The RFC has therefore migrated the signature ciphersuite to RSA-SHA256. The NULL ciphersuite is intentionally weak and suitable only for environments where stronger cryptography is unavailable or the threat model does not require authentication; it provides no protection against active attacks.
sections.eli5: The signature protects against forgery, and the cookie protects against replays and floods. Together they make deep-space messages much safer. But keys still have to be loaded onto the spacecraft before launch, because there is no time to negotiate during the mission.

sections.title: Ciphersuite Details
sections.content:
HMAC-SHA1-80: Uses HMAC with the SHA-1 hash algorithm. The AuthVal field contains the output of the HMAC-SHA1-80 algorithm, which is a fixed 10 octets (80 bits, hence the name). The key is pre-shared between communicating LTP engines. This ciphersuite is suitable for mutual authentication when both sides possess the same secret key.

RSA-SHA256: Uses RSA signatures with SHA-256. The AuthVal field contains the RSA signature value, which occupies the minimum number of octets required (e.g., 128 octets for a 1024-bit RSA key). This ciphersuite provides asymmetric authentication; the receiver needs only the public key, while the sender needs the private key. NULL: Uses a hardcoded HMAC key (defined in the RFC) and produces the same output as HMAC-SHA1-80. It provides no confidentiality or authentication; its only purpose is to detect accidental corruption, similar to a CRC.
sections.eli5: HMAC is like a secret code both sides share; only they can make or check the signature. RSA is like a lock and key: the receiver keeps a public part of the lock, the sender has the private key. NULL is like a simple checksum, good only for catching accidents, not attacks.

items.label: HMAC-SHA1-80
items.desc: HMAC with SHA-1 hash; 10-octet authentication value. Uses pre-shared key.

items.label: RSA-SHA256
items.desc: RSA signature with SHA-256 hash. Asymmetric authentication; signature length depends on key size.

items.label: NULL
items.desc: Hardcoded HMAC key; provides only checksum, no real authentication.
